extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Christian apologetics and biblical exegesis (clergy, theologians, informed lay readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for interpreting Scripture and for using prophecy as proof of Christianity; focuses on reconciling apparent contradictions, distinguishing literal and spiritual senses, and assessing prophetic fulfilment and specificity as evidential criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types (typical meaning vs literal reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter kills. All happened in types. Christ must suffer. An humiliated God. Circumcision of the heart, true fasting, true sacrifice, a true temple. The prophets have shown that all these must be spiritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the law, sacrifices, and kingdom cannot be applied to literal reality they are to be understood as types foreshadowing spiritual realities. Examples from Scripture: 'Not the meat which perishes, but that which does not perish.' 'Ye shall be free indeed'—the former freedom was only a type. Treat Old Testament institutions as typological when literal application leads to contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile contradictory passages (contradiction criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only describe a good character by reconciling all contrary qualities... To understand the meaning of an author, we must make all the contrary passages agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound interpretation of Scripture must provide a sense in which even apparently contradictory passages are reconciled. It is insufficient for a meaning to suit many concordant passages; it must reconcile the contradictory ones as well. If no reconciling sense exists, the text would lack meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal falsehood implies spiritual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: When the word of God, which is really true, is false literally, it is true spiritually. 'Sede a dextris meis:' this is false literally, therefore it is true spiritually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an anthropomorphic or literal reading of divine language would be false (e.g., ascribing human modes of action to God), interpret the phrase spiritually as indicating God's intention or analogous relation rather than a literal mode of being. Use this principle for passages describing God in human terms ('jealous God', 'received the odour of your incense').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invent unrevealed mystical meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not allowable to attribute to Scripture the meaning which is not revealed to us; thus, to say that the closed mem of Isaiah signifies six hundred has not been revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speculative or arbitrary mystical etymologies, numerologies, or letter-symbolism not attested by revelation. You may hypothesize mysteries, but do not assert hidden literal senses unless they have been divinely revealed or warranted by the prophetic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let decisive clear sayings fix ambiguous passages
rubrics_metrics.description: One saying of David, or of Moses... enables us to judge of their spirit. If all their other expressions were ambiguous, and left us in doubt... one saying of this kind would in fact determine all the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an author (or prophetic corpus) contains clear, unambiguous statements that settle a doctrinal or thematic point, use those to determine the meaning of otherwise ambiguous or double-meaning passages. A single decisive sentence can resolve interpretive doubt across the rest of the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve lexical ambiguity by cross‑contextual usage
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of two persons... uses language with a double meaning... but afterwards one says angelic things, and the other always dull commonplaces, he will judge that the one spoke in mysteries, and not the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare usages across authors and contexts: when the same term elsewhere clearly denotes one sense (e.g., 'enemies' meaning 'sins'), apply that sense to ambiguous occurrences. Preference is given to the usage consistent with the author's overall spiritual character or confirmed meaning elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecies as the strongest proof of Christ's divinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophecies are the strongest proof of Jesus Christ. It is for them also that God has made most provision; for the event which has fulfilled them is a miracle existing since the birth of the Church to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fulfilment of prophecy as primary apologetic evidence. The argument emphasises that prophets and prophecies were prepared and dispersed by God over long periods to make the Messiah's coming credibly foretold and to distinguish fulfillment from chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity, succession, and distribution of prophecies increase evidential weight
rubrics_metrics.description: If one man alone had made a book of predictions about Jesus Christ... there is much more here. Here is a succession of men during four thousand years... Here is a whole people who announce it, and who have existed for four thousand years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidential strength rises with: (a) multiple independent predictors, (b) succession of prophets across generations, and (c) a people who preserve and carry prophecies across the world. These factors reduce the plausibility of chance or fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific/particular predictions strengthen prophetic confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictions of particular things: they were strangers in Egypt... Joseph, when dying, bade his children carry his bones with them... Moses assigned to each family portions of that land before they entered it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight prophecies that predict particular, verifiable events or unlikely circumstances (e.g., exile details, family fortunes, burial instructions). The intermingling of such particular predictions with Messianic prophecies increases overall confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrence of diverse prophetic measures and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The time foretold by the state of the Jewish people, by the state of the heathen, by the state of the temple, by the number of years... It was necessary that the four idolatrous or pagan monarchies, the end of the kingdom of Judah, and the seventy weeks, should happen at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust prophetic scheme requires several independent chronological or political indicators (national/state conditions, foreign monarchies, temple status, explicit time periods) to coincide. Convergence of different prophetic methods on the same timeframe strengthens claim of divine foreknowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecies often only recognized after events (retrospective understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: We understand the prophecies only when we see the events happen... The proofs of retreat, discretion, silence, etc. are proofs only to those who know and believe them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many prophetic texts are obscure until fulfillment clarifies them. Use historical events that match prophetic markers to interpret and validate earlier ambiguous texts; prophetic insights may be sealed or hidden until realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outward rites subordinate to inward disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the meat which perishes, but that which does not perish... Outward sacrifice is not the essential point... Circumcision of the heart, true fasting, true sacrifice, a true temple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret sacrificial and ritual prescriptions as meaningful only insofar as they reflect inner spiritual disposition. Scriptural commands about rites may be typological or disciplinary, not ultimate ends; Jeremiah and other prophets reject mere externalism (e.g., 'What avails it you to add sacrifice to sacrifice?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fulfillment across nations and history as evidence (prophetic preservation and worldwide distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: But it was not enough that the prophecies should exist. It was necessary that they should be distributed throughout all places, and preserved throughout all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An argument for divine origin appeals to the fact that prophecies were preserved by a people (the Jews) and carried into many lands, making prediction accessible across times and places—supporting the universal claim of the Gospel and protecting against the appearance of local coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret prophetic language of reprobation and calling as thematic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprobation of the Jews and conversion of the Gentiles... 'I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not'... 'I have spread out my hands all the day unto an unbelieving people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prophetic fulfilment not only by discrete events but by large themes (e.g., the Jewish people's rejection and the Gentile calling). The fulfilment of these broad prophetic themes across history functions as corroborative evidence for Messianic claims.
